newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto seen reaching truce in feud with president.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto seen reaching truce in feud with president.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto appeared to have reached a truce with President Farooq Leghari on Saturday as the two met for more than six hours after weeks of simmering differences between them.
Both "expressed satisfaction over the meeting and decided to continue such meetings as before", an official statement said afterwards.

The prime minister, still reeling from the shock of the death of her estranged younger brother Murtaza Bhutto in a shootout with police last week, met the president amid growing speculation that he might sack her government and order fresh elections because of opposition charges of official corruption.
The statement said the two leaders would meet next after Bhutto returns from a visit to the United States, a decision that appeared to signal a temporary peace between them.
The prime minister leaves for New York on Sunday, primarily to address the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
The statement said Bhutto "agreed with the spirit" of a suggestion from Leghari that parliamentary committees be formed to fight corruption.

Leghari sent a rare message to parliament on Monday urging the government and the opposition parties to cooperate in setting up parliamentary committees to tackle corruption. "I feel the time for action has come," he said.
Leghari also proposed several changes to the existing laws dealing with corruption and suggested an amendment to bar those found guilty of misconduct from public office for seven years.

Bhutto, speaking at a mourning meeting for her brother on Thursday, made an apparent reference to the president's actions, alleging that there was a conspiracy against her government being implemented "under a timetable".
Leghari retorted on Friday by asking unspecified holders of public office to refrain from making "unwarranted and irresponsible" statements.
The indirect exchanges were the first of the type between the two leaders since they were both elected to their offices in 1993 as members of the Pakistan People's Party led by Bhutto.
A week ago Leghari openly aired his differences with Bhutto over the issue of judicial appointments by officially asking the Supreme Court for a delineation of his powers in the matter.
This was done only a day after the shootout in the port city of Karachi in which Bhutto's brother and seven other members of his breakaway Shaheed Bhutto faction of the PPP were killed.
Leghari also met opposition leader Nawaz Sharif on Thursday and told him he would use his discretionary powers to dismiss the government if he found it to be in "the supreme national interest".
Supporters of Murtaza accuse police of ambushing and killing their leader near his Karachi home. Police say they fired in self-defence after Murtaza's bodyguards started shooting.
The government has ordered a judicial inquiry.
